definition: Rescind means to officially cancel a law, order, or agreement, usually through a deliberate, formal act by a governing body.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rescind. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rescind should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Facing public outcry, the school board voted to rescind its new dress code just two weeks after adopting it.
To suspend a rule is only to pause it for a time, while to rescind it is to cancel it outright.
Rescinding an order wipes it off the books going forward, but expunging a record erases every trace that it ever existed.

Repeal means to officially cancel a law, and only a law: legislatures repeal the statutes and ordinances they or their predecessors enacted. Rescind covers more ground — a council, board, or company can rescind an order, a policy, an offer, or an agreement, not just legislation. Every repeal cancels a law; you cannot repeal a job offer.

Retract means to take back something one has said or written — a claim, a comment, an accusation — usually admitting it was wrong. Rescind is institutional: a body formally cancels an order, offer, policy, or agreement it had made. A columnist retracts a statement; a school board rescinds a policy.

Rescind means to officially cancel a law, order, or agreement, usually through a deliberate, formal act by a governing body.
In March, the village council approved an ordinance charging residents for overnight street parking.
Complaints flooded in from nurses and factory workers who came home long after every garage had closed.
At its next session, the council held a formal vote to rescind the ordinance, striking it from the books entirely.
The fee disappeared, and the parking rules returned to exactly what they had been before March.
A governing body used a formal vote to cancel an order it had previously issued, which is exactly what rescind means.
formal, legal/parliamentary register
Rescind is the standard verb for a council, board, or agency formally canceling its own ordinance, order, or offer (rescind an ordinance, rescind a job offer).

Rescind is close to revoke, which specifically cancels a right, privilege, or official document, often as a punishment, and to invalidate, which makes something no longer legally binding, sometimes because of a flaw rather than a deliberate act; never treat the three as interchangeable.

In March the museum's board approved a two-year loan of its Vermeer to a gallery overseas, and the paperwork was signed before Easter.
Then engineers inspecting the gallery's new wing found the climate controls failing badly on humid days.
Under the loan's own terms, either party could cancel if the painting's safety came into doubt.
So in June the board voted, formally and unanimously, to rescind the agreement altogether; the crates were unpacked and the Vermeer went back on its wall at home.
The gallery has invited the board to sign a fresh loan once the climate system passes a full year of testing, but the old agreement itself is dead — cancelled, not shelved.
